prompt: What did the State of DevOps research find about speed and stability?

choices.text: That teams must choose one and give up the other
choices.why: That was the belief the research tested and did not find.

choices.text: That stability matters only for large companies
choices.why: The finding held across sizes and kinds of software.

choices.text: That they rise and fall together
choices.why: Right. The teams that delivered most often also failed least and recovered fastest.

choices.text: That speed always comes at the cost of more incidents
choices.why: The data showed the opposite.

prompt: Match each DORA metric to the kind of thing it measures.
Why does this course quote no DORA performance thresholds, such as what counts as elite?

choices.text: Its own trend teaches a team more
choices.why: Right. The thresholds describe other organisations and change each year; lesson 6 develops why.

choices.text: The thresholds are secret
choices.why: They are published in each report.

choices.text: The thresholds only apply to Google
choices.why: They come from a survey of many organisations.

choices.text: Thresholds were abolished in 2018
choices.why: Reports kept publishing clusters after 2018.

prompt: What did the 2023 report rename time to restore as, and why?

choices.text: Mean time between failures, to measure reliability
choices.why: That is a different measure, about how often failures happen.

choices.text: Incident duration, to include every outage
choices.why: The rename went the other way, towards deployments only.

choices.text: Rework rate, to count fixes
choices.why: Rework rate is the 2024 addition, a separate measure.

choices.text: Failed deployment recovery time
choices.why: Right. It recovers from a deployment, not from any outage.

prompt: A change merges on Friday and is deployed on Thursday. When was it delivered?

choices.text: On Friday, when it merged
choices.why: Merged code waiting for a train has not reached users.

choices.text: On Thursday
choices.why: Right. A deployment is a change reaching the environment users use.

choices.text: When it was first deployed to a test environment
choices.why: Test environments do not count as delivery.

choices.text: When its pull request was opened
choices.why: That is somewhere near the start of lead time, not delivery.

prompt: A team deploys more often this quarter and has more failed deployments than last quarter. Can its change failure rate have gone down?

choices.text: No, more failures always means a higher rate
choices.why: The rate divides by deployments, which rose too.

choices.text: No, because the rate counts incidents per month
choices.why: It is a share of deployments, not a monthly count.

choices.text: Yes, if deployments grew faster than failures
choices.why: Right. Three failures in sixty is a lower rate than two in twenty.

choices.text: Only if time to restore went down too
choices.why: The two are independent measurements.

prompt: When is service restored, for time to restore?

choices.text: When users are no longer affected
choices.why: Right. A rollback restores; finding the cause is not required.

choices.text: When the bug that caused it is fixed and deployed
choices.why: That often comes much later than the restore.

choices.text: When the postmortem is written
choices.why: The postmortem comes days later; lesson 15.

choices.text: When the incident channel is archived
choices.why: Archiving is housekeeping, not recovery.

prompt: A team switches from counting one deployment per release to one per service, and it has five services. What happens to its deployment frequency?

choices.text: Nothing, because the same code reached production
choices.why: The code is the same; the count is not.

choices.text: It falls, because releases are now split
choices.why: Splitting one into five raises the count.

choices.text: It becomes impossible to compute
choices.why: It is still a count; just a different one.

choices.text: It jumps up to five times, with nothing really changed
choices.why: Right. That is why the definition is written down and changed only with a note.

prompt: Which of these count as a change failure in this course's definition? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A deployment rolled back because it broke card charges
choices.why: Right. A failure in production needing remediation.

choices.text: A deployment followed by a hotfix for the bug it introduced
choices.why: Right. The hotfix is the remediation.

choices.text: A pull request that failed its tests and never merged
choices.why: It never reached production, so it is not a deployment at all.

choices.text: A deployment whose feature nobody ended up using
choices.why: Unwanted is not broken; that is a question about value, not stability.

prompt: In June and July the Billing team made 9 deployments and 2 failed. What was the change failure rate, to the nearest whole percent?
Why did the Billing team's failed deployments take more than two hours to undo before August?

choices.text: The team had no rollback tooling until August
choices.why: Nothing in the history says the tooling changed.

choices.text: Each carried six to eight changes to untangle
choices.why: Right. Somebody had to find the wrong change before rolling anything back.

choices.text: Thursday afternoons had fewer people available
choices.why: The program does not model who was around.

choices.text: Failures were only noticed on the next day
choices.why: Restore times were measured in minutes from the deployment.

prompt: Nobody on the Billing team set out to improve the change failure rate. Why did it fall anyway?

choices.text: Because they added more automated tests in August
choices.why: Nothing about tests changed in the history.

choices.text: Because Bia started reviewing more carefully
choices.why: After August Bia did fewer reviews, not more careful ones.

choices.text: Smaller open work made smaller batches per deployment
choices.why: Right. Speed and stability moved together because both depend on batch size.

choices.text: Because failures are counted differently after August
choices.why: The same rule applies across the whole history.

prompt: July has 5 deployments and 1 failed. How should a report state that?

choices.text: One of five failed
choices.why: Right. Below twenty or thirty deployments, the count is more honest than a rate.

choices.text: A change failure rate of 20.0%
choices.why: A decimal on five events claims a precision it does not have.

choices.text: Too few deployments to say anything at all
choices.why: The count is worth saying; the rate is what is fragile.

choices.text: A rate in line with the industry average
choices.why: Comparing five events to an industry figure says nothing.

prompt: In September the Billing team made 20 deployments in 30 days. How many deployments a week is that, to one decimal place?
Why does dora.py report medians for lead time and time to restore, but a rate for failures?

choices.text: Medians are easier to compute than averages
choices.why: Ease is not the reason; shape is.

choices.text: Failures cannot be averaged
choices.why: A rate is in fact an average of ones and zeros.

choices.text: The DORA reports forbid averages
choices.why: No such rule; it is a choice about tails.

choices.text: Durations have long tails; failures are a share
choices.why: Right. A few long recoveries would dominate an average.

prompt: Where should a single team get its deployment frequency from?

choices.text: From a survey asking each person how often they deploy
choices.why: That asks for an estimate of a fact a machine already recorded.

choices.text: From the pipeline's own records
choices.why: Right. Read the systems; do not survey the people.

choices.text: From the number of tickets closed
choices.why: Closed tickets are not deployments.

choices.text: From the DORA report for its industry
choices.why: That describes other organisations.

prompt: Why should a team decide what counts as a failure before looking at its numbers?

choices.text: Because the DORA reports require it
choices.why: It is about honesty with yourself, not about a report.

choices.text: Because failures cannot be counted afterwards
choices.why: They can; the risk is how the ambiguous ones get counted.

choices.text: Late rules drift towards the flattering reading
choices.why: Right. Nobody intends it; it is how people read ambiguous rules.

choices.text: Because the definition changes the incident's severity
choices.why: Severity is decided by impact, lesson 13.

prompt: A team measures lead time for changes from the merge. Which problem can that number never show?

choices.text: A queue in front of review
choices.why: Right. Review happens before the merge, so the clock starts after it.

choices.text: A slow pipeline
choices.why: The pipeline runs after the merge, inside the measurement.

choices.text: A weekly release train
choices.why: The wait for the train is after the merge too.

choices.text: A failed deployment
choices.why: Failures are a different metric, not hidden by this choice.

prompt: Match each metric to the system its timing comes from.
Accelerate, the 2018 book about the research, was written by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene ___.
A quarterly report shows deployment frequency and lead time for changes, both improving, and nothing else. What is missing?

choices.text: The number of story points delivered
choices.why: Points are not a DORA metric and do not balance speed.

choices.text: The two stability metrics
choices.why: Right. Speed alone is easy to improve by not caring whether deployments fail.

choices.text: A comparison with the industry's elite cluster
choices.why: That would add someone else's numbers, not the missing half.

choices.text: The names of the developers who deployed
choices.why: Delivery metrics describe the system, not people.

prompt: A team's last 40 deployments include 6 that needed a rollback or hotfix. What is its change failure rate, in percent?
Put the moments in a change's life in order, as the lesson's timeline draws them.
A team's time to restore is measured from when an incident was declared. The median looks excellent. What may it be hiding?

choices.text: Failed deployments that were never rolled back
choices.why: Those still have a restore time, by fix rather than rollback.

choices.text: The time spent writing the postmortem
choices.why: That was never part of time to restore.

choices.text: Deployments made outside working hours
choices.why: Hours of the day do not move a duration's start.

choices.text: Slow detection before anyone declared it
choices.why: Right. Starting at the declaration leaves out the part that is often largest; lesson 14.
